events.description: Complex Taliban attack on Combat Outpost Keating in Kamdesh. Eight US troops were killed and 26 wounded, and the outpost was nearly overrun and later burned. The hosts argue that foreign jihadists (Arabs, Uzbeks, possibly Chechens) took part alongside the Taliban.
Captain Keating dies when a heavy truck falls off a cliff road and explodes. The outpost is renamed after him.
US counterinsurgency operations in Kunar and Nuristan, 2006-2009, followed by a withdrawal from the area around 2008-2009.
Osama bin Laden ordered al-Qaeda personnel out of northern Pakistan into Kunar, Nuristan and other parts of Afghanistan.
Qari Ziyaur Rahman was reported dead, but later reappeared to deny it.
Earlier battle, about a year before Keating, in which US forces were surrounded and nearly overrun at Wana; about 9 killed (the host says 'I believe 25').
The US Army announced it was discontinuing the Asymmetric Warfare Group and the Rapid Equipping Force as it shifts from counterinsurgency to large-scale combat operations.
Hillary Clinton said the US had broken the Taliban's momentum; a Guardian report said both sides were tired.
Obama said in the State of the Union that the Taliban's momentum had been broken.
Leon Panetta called green-on-blue attacks the 'last gasp' of the Taliban.
US-Taliban deal in Doha, after which the Taliban launched large operations against the Afghan government.
Benghazi attack involving AQAP, AQIM, Ansar al-Sharia and the Muhammad Jamal Network, per a Senate Intelligence Committee report. The date is not stated in this chunk.
Panetta called green-on-blue insider attacks evidence of the 'last gasp' of the Taliban; hosts say 'eight years later'.
General Campbell said the Taliban were tired from 14 years of fighting and wanted to get on with their lives.
Dana White called the Taliban 'desperate'.
DOJ announced 27 ISIS fighters or associates had been repatriated from SDF custody to the US, including Imran and Jihad Ali.
Imran Ali and his family moved to Syria to join ISIS, per charging documents.
The Alis surrendered to the SDF near Baghuz.
Awlaki was killed in a US drone strike; hosts say about 10 years earlier.
ISIS spokesman al-Adnani was killed; hosts say 'a couple years ago'.

key_claims: Kunar and Nuristan were al-Qaeda hotbeds when COP Keating was attacked in 2009, with dual-hatted commanders such as Qari Ziyaur Rahman and Faruq al-Qahtani.

Roggio argues the Keating attack was a complex assault with foreign fighters (Arabs, Uzbeks, possibly 'Chechens') alongside the Taliban, citing the fighters' headbands, kit quality, accuracy and grenade launchers on AKs. The US military and the film call the attackers simply 'Taliban'.
Taliban shadow governor Dost Muhammad in Nuristan was closely allied with al-Qaeda and worked with al-Qahtani and Qari Ziyaur Rahman.
LeT, JeM, Jamaat al-Dawa al-Quran and the TTP all operate in or raid into Kunar and Nuristan alongside the Taliban and al-Qaeda.
Films such as The Outpost, 13 Hours and Lone Survivor leave out al-Qaeda's role, although evidence ties al-Qaeda to Benghazi, Black Hawk Down and Lone Survivor.
The 'tired Taliban' talking point dates to 2004 and has been repeated by US officials (Clinton 2011, Obama 2012, Panetta 2012, Trump) with no battlefield evidence.
The Taliban has a safe haven in Pakistan, and to a lesser extent Iran, and remains allied with al-Qaeda.
US officials repeatedly misjudged the Taliban, with 'last gasp', 'tired' and 'desperate' claims made from 2012 to 2018.
The claim that the Taliban is purely nationalist is rebutted by its own statements, its foreign-jihadist videos, and its acceptance of Zawahiri's oath.
Anwar al-Awlaki's online lectures continue to radicalize English speakers, many of whom go on to join ISIS despite his al-Qaeda affiliation.
ISIS used Awlaki's material in propaganda and named an English-speaking battalion after him in Syria.
Per the bin Laden files, Awlaki was senior enough that AQAP's emir suggested he lead the group, but bin Laden declined.
Al-Qaeda has had no English-language ideologue as effective as Awlaki since his death, though ISIS adapted its messaging and social media without one.
The FBI has had hundreds or thousands of ISIS-related cases, and a wider support network likely stands behind the visible volunteers.
